scenario: AITA for telling my mom not to touch my things? | Not sure how to start this off. My mom and I dont have a good relationship at all, ever since I've moved in with my boyfriend it's gotten better. But not really. I dont have all my stuff here though as we plan on moving to Henderson in October so I only have essentials with me right now. Today, I am going to my school to get pictures for the virtual graduation next month, and I want my flute with me. My flute is my everything. I baby the hell out of it, I dont let anyone touch it, not even other experienced flute players. It's currently at my mom's house and she KNOWS I never want her to touch it. Not even if it's in the case. It's not my old student model that was only $800. This one is an Azumi Atlus, a professional model. She likes to make the excuse that she helped me get it, in a way yes. Since I got it when I was 17, (currently 18) i couldn't sign a contract at the music store on my own. So my mom signed for it in her name and payment plans were set up. However. I paid for it. Within 10 months (on a 12 month plan) I paid off $2,316. On my own. My solid silver baby was finally mine. It bumped my mom's credit up too especially since I paid it off early. Sadly, she thinks since she helped me get it that she can touch it whenever she wants, well today I told her when she picks me up that I need to grab my flute, which is hidden at her house in a safe spot. She said she could just bring it and I firmly said no. Now, she won't stop calling me and texting me demanding to tell her where it is and that "I got it for you, I can touch it whenever I want." she thinks I'm disrespectful for not letting her touch my very delicate and expensive instrument. AITA?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I need to figure out if the action in this scenario is morally acceptable. The user is asking if they're "AITA" (Am I the Asshole) for telling their mom not to touch their flute. Let me break this down.

First, the background: The person has a strained relationship with their mom. They moved in with their boyfriend, which improved things a bit, but it's still not great. They don't have all their stuff there because they're planning to move soon. The main issue is their flute, which is very important to them. It's a professional model, an Azumi Atlus, which is expensive and delicate. They paid off the $2,316 for it on their own, even though their mom signed the contract because they were 17 at the time.

Now, the mom thinks she can touch the flute because she helped get it, but the person doesn't want anyone, even experienced players, to touch it. Today, the person needed their flute for school pictures and told their mom not to bring it, fearing she might touch it. The mom is upset, calling and texting, saying she can touch it because she helped get it, and the person is being disrespectful.

So, the question is: Is it morally acceptable for the person to tell their mom not to touch their flute?

I think the key points here are ownership, respect, and boundaries. The person owns the flute, having paid it off entirely. They have a right to set boundaries about who can touch it, especially since it's delicate and expensive. The mom's argument is that she helped get it, but the person paid for it, so the ownership is clear.

However, the mom might feel entitled because she signed the contract and it's tied to her credit. But the person took responsibility to pay it off early, which also helped her credit. So, the mom's claim is more emotional than financial.

The person's action of setting a boundary is about protecting their property and their emotional attachment. It's reasonable to not want someone to touch something so important, especially if there's a history of the mom not respecting their wishes.

On the other hand, the mom might feel disrespected because she feels she contributed to getting the flute. But the person's right to set boundaries about their belongings should take precedence. It's about personal property rights and emotional well-being.

So, considering all this, the action of telling the mom not to touch the flute is morally acceptable because it's about protecting one's own property and setting personal boundaries, even if the mom feels entitled.
